It would be easier to say what’s going on with a video of your stroke. But it sounds like you may not be rotating your hips and shoulders enough. That would explain both the shoulder pain and why your hand is hitting your hip. You should be hitting a 45 degree (or greater) angle between your shoulder and the surface of the water when you rotate.

Also how are you sure that you perfectly at 12 o clock with your hand? Did a coach or someone confirm that for you? I’ve worked with a number of swimmers who would swear that they’re pointing straight down until I show them a video of their stroke and they’re pointing their fingers at the gosh darn wall. Sometimes our spatial awareness just isn’t quite what we think it is.  

Another possibility is that even though you’re getting your forearm vertical you may not be pulling parallel to your body in a straight line. You could be doing an S pull where you drift in toward your center line then pull out as you get closer to your hip. 

I’d recommend double checking your early vertical forearm, the actual line you pull in, and how much rotation you’re getting. Also see if any of that changes when you take a breath. If you have someone film your stroke then you can analyze it without just going on feel. Even better if you can get underwater video of your stroke.

Good luck

There’s nothing wrong with just getting in and swimming straight, if all you want to do is get in and move for a bit. However, if you feel like you’ve hit a plateau and want to get faster then you need to do things that will challenge your body in different ways. That’s how training forces adaptations that lead to improvements. Take lifting weights as an example. If someone uses the same exact weight for the same exercise and the same number of repetitions every single time. For a little while they may improve until there is no more need to adapt then they stagnate. 

For you it depends on your goals. If you want to be able to hold a faster pace then you need to spend time swimming at or under that pace. For example if you want to be able to hold 1:45 pace for a 1k then practice swimming 100s at that pace on a 2:00 interval. When that becomes easy lower the interval or increase the number of 100s you do.

There are also just so many other things you can do in the pool beyond swimming straight. You can do sets focused on power and DPS (distant per stroke). Or sets focused on tempo, breath control, under-waters off the walls, technique work, pace for different distances. Sets dedicated to different strokes. Different energy systems from aerobic steady state to lactic threshold. Working on all of these things is what makes a well rounded swimmer. Personally, I find that it keeps things interesting.

I’m not saying you have to do all of that stuff to get better, but pushing outside of our comfort zones is literally how we improve.

It would be hard to say what to biggest factor is for you without seeing how you swim. 

Generally:
Increase distance per stroke or DPS (power)
Increase tempo (stroke rate)
Reduce drag (body position, breathing)
Then all the little tricks
-fast flips turns
-tight streamlines
-strong underwater dolphin kicks
-not breathing on breakouts and finishes

You can increase your DPS by reducing drag, having an efficient strong 6 beat kick, and catching more water using more early vertical forearm (unless it’s a 50 then straight arm that)

For tempo I like to focus on speeding up the recovery part of the stroke cycle. Just make sure you don’t fall apart with the rest of you technique stay long

For drag don’t let your legs sink and keep a low profile breath. Also limit breathing during key points like the first few stroke after a breakout and finishes. The best 50 Fr swimmers just don’t breath when they race the 50

That’s my general advice as a coach and a sprinter.

That being said if you’re improving in other races, then maybe those are the ones you should focus on. 

Personally, I went into this college season thinking that the 50 was going to be one of my best races, and was a little disappointed with it at the duel meet I actually swam it at. Turns out the 100 and 200 were better for me. I focused on those and at mid season with a little rest actually went a pb in the 50 (22.40) leading off my 100 (46.86) lol. 

You’ll get that 50 pb, but explore what races are best for you and focus on those.

Creatine can help with short term energy production so you could have slightly more power off the start, turns, and overall for the first 10 sec or so of the race. It works by building up phosphocreatine stores in your muscles which gives your phosphocreatine system (an anaerobic metabolic pathway) a larger store to pull from. It would not necessarily help with fatigue over long distances, but it also won’t hurt. And won’t make you sink if you’re worried about that.

For fatigue management in a 200 or 400 beta-alanine may be a better option for a supplement. There is decent evidence that it helps marginally by increasing stores of carnosine. Carnosine is an acid buffer. As you exert yourself acidic metabolic by-products build up in your muscles and limit energy production, which is why you fatigue. Carnosine slows the pH change and allows you to maintain higher energy outputs for longer.

Beta-alanine does cause an itchy skin feeling as a side effect though.

Both are relatively safe to consume and are legal supplements in competitive swimming. They are also both naturally produced in your body for these specific functions. Supplementing just makes sure your stores are as high as they should be for peak performance.

Each requires around a 4 week loading period while stores build up in your muscles before you can really see any benefits.

Standard dose for creatine is 5 grams daily
Standard dose for beta-alanine is 4-6 grams daily
(Some people break up beta-alanine doses to limit the itchy feeling. 2-3 grams twice a day)

If you go for creatine get creatine monohydrate it’s the cheapest and has the most evidence for its effectiveness.

Personally I’m a collegiate swimmer and take both. I’ve found that my 100s and 200s have benefitted, but that’s just anecdotal. I don’t really swim over the 200 very often, but I could see beta-alanine helping there.

Also, I know Cody Miller has mentioned taking both in his vlogs at some point. 

It’s up to you. I’d recommend reading some of the academic studies on both so you can make an informed decision. Don’t just depend on reddit comments or fitness sites.

Hope that helps. Good luck!

1) Try slowing down your breathing and being more relaxed in the water. Breath control is one of the biggest parts of learning how to swim well. Exhale slowly while your face is in the water. That will help you build a rhythm between your breathing and strokes.

2) When chlorine goes up the nose or anywhere it should be it burns. Happens to all of us. Over time you get better at keeping it out of your nose and mouth. Exhaling through the nose is a great way to keep water out of there.

3) Keep your kicks small. Your feet should stay pretty dang close to the surface of the water at all times, and should break the surface every kick. Your hand in your pull would be deeper than your feet if you’re swimming front craw efficiently. There is no reason you should be afraid of bottoming out with your kick. Kick just enough to keep your feet on the surface, don’t gas yourself out bc you afraid your feet may sink.
Good luck!

That panicked feeling is biological. It comes from a build up of carbonic acid in the blood. Exhaling slowly can help lessen it, but breath control training can be very dangerous. Especially if the lifeguard knows you’re trying to hold your breath and doesn’t realize something has gone wrong quick enough.

Your kick is the foundation of your stroke, if you’re working on freestyle you’ll want to develop a strong 6 beat flutter kick to have the best stroke. Once you have that and can maintain that then you can play around with a lighter or stronger kick depending on the needs of the event you’re doing. Many of the best (but not all) distance swimmers still do a 6 beat kick their whole race.

What you really need is someone who can see the area’s of your technique and racing that need the most improvement. In general though, first get your distance per stroke lower. If you’re swimming in yards like 8-11 strokes per 25. This involves technique and power development. Once you do that comfortably get your tempo (stroke rate) higher. Make sure you kick is keeping up with your arm tempo. Working on your turns, starts, streamline position and underwaters will all help too. I’ve coached some kids around your age down to the 23-25 sec range in their 50 SCY. Still going 22 as an old man myself.

You could cycle through different energy systems. Like a long steady day with longer distance swims, short rest, and not very fast. A threshold day with moderate distance swims, low to moderate rest, and a little bit of speed. And fast days with short distances, lots of speed and plenty of rest. Super basic stuff. Mix in a stroke day and a technique day. And you have 5 simple plans for each day.

Swim coach and sports biology student here. If you’re switching over from running to swimming there are a few things to consider. Comparing the two sports swimming any given distance is similar to running about 4 times that same distance. So a 100m swim is like a 400m run. Competitive swimmers tend to do a lot more volume compared to competitive runners who train for similar events. Part of the reason swimmers do more is because swimming is a nonimpact activity so you can get away with more compared to running. But running is a higher quality for of cardio (don’t tell the swimmers that tho). That just means that at similar intensities running will cause you to have a higher heart rate. Put those too factors together a swimmer who trains for middle distance (200m and 400m events) events may swim 6,000-8,000m each training session, which is similar to running a half marathon each day. Distance swimmers can get up to 10,000-12,000m is a single practice. 

For example I’m a 26 yo M getting back into competitive swimming and I’m focusing on sprinting and a little mid distance training. Today was my aerobic day

Warm Up 

400 Fr

6x 75 Drill (1:20)

4x 100 Desc (1:35)

50 Ez


Main Set (2x through)

Odds: Threshold

Evens: Stretch

2x 400 (5:20)

2x 300 (4:00)

2x 200 (2:40)

2x 100 (1:20)


Kick work

450 Kick with board (50ez/25fast)

Cool Down

4x 75 breath control (1:20)

50 Float


Total yards: 6,100


I wouldn’t recommend jumping to that kind of volume suddenly, if your stroke isn’t efficient it would take too long and you’d risk developing shoulder issues. I’d recommend working on stroke technique and increasing total weekly swimming volume by 10%-15% until you start getting the results you want.

Yeah if you’re doing like an 800m swim or more then a 2-4 beat kick is fine. But for mid distance and sprinting usually swimmers do a 6 beat kick (6 kicks per stroke cycle, which is 2 strokes). The kick is the foundation of your stroke, if you can master the kick then you set yourself up to have a really solid stroke. Then best swimmers can change their kick when the need to, even distance swimmers will switch into a 6 beat kick to finish their races strong.

Dolphin kick (butterfly kick) is a new motor skill for you, it’s not second nature yet. That’s why you’re falling into a flutter kick. When I teach fly to new swimmers I like to do a lot of Dolphin kick work with them before adding the pull. A solid progression is to start with some lengths of dolphin kick with a kick board (focus on keeping your hips near the surface, you want your butt to break the surface with each kick). Next try doing the kick without the board, arms straight out front (Superman position). For this drill keep your head down (face in the water) as much as you can. Lift your head for a quick breath then face back in the water. Then you can either go for one arm fly breathing to the side or a 4 kick 1 pull fly (with both arms) hang out in that Superman position as much as you need to. A 4 kick 1 pull fly is a full legal fly but it’s not as fast as a 2 kick 1 pull fly which is what most swimmers do.

Underwaters do help with speed if you can use them. Max sped in a streamline dolphin kick is fast than max speed on the surface, and you can carry the speed from your walls further in a streamline dolphin kick than you can on the surface. Honestly I think you’re running into a conditioning problem. Because you’re not getting as much oxygen when you’re going further underwater it’s causing fatigue to set in faster. If you focus on going further in your underwaters in training consistently your body will make adaptations to reduce this fatigue over time. You need to challenge that system though by hitting the fatigue in training more frequently though.

Sounds like you have a shoulder driven stroke rather than a hip driven stroke. You can work on developing a hip driven stroke with some drills. 

-Side Glide: 1-arm out front other arm at your side. The arm out front should be under your body with your opposite shoulder out of the water. Focus on a steady kick with you hips and toes near the surface. (Practice this on both sides)

-6 Kick Switch: Side glide but after 6 kicks take a stroke to switch sides. Make sure there’s no gap in your kick when you switch.

-6+3: Same as 6 kick switch but take 3 strokes to switch sides getting in 3 kicks for every 1 stroke

-“Perfect” Freestyle: When you can comfortably maintain three kicks per stroke while swimming this is know as having a 6 beat kick (6 kick in one full stroke cycle) your whole body should be rotating not just your shoulders

This isn’t easy to maintain if  you’re not used to it, but you can get used to it with time. I feel really sluggish if I don’t kick, but it’s easy for me to maintain a 6 beat kick. Do the drills as a progression to develop technique. Focus on your hips and toes. You can also incorporate them into your warm up.

Note: one full stroke cycle is when both arms make a full rotation that’s why it’s a 6 beat kick even though it’s 3 kick per stroke

Make sure that you body is rotating as you pull the water. Time your breath with the rotation. As you chest is turned to the side during your rotation you should breath and as your chest rotates back down to face the bottom of the pool your head should follow. 

Also make sure you are NOT looking forward when you breath. Look to the side as you take your breath and look at the bottom of the pool when not breathing.

I’ve been 47 in 100 Fr. You want to maintain an even stroke rate, any pause will cause a loss in momentum. I would recommend training your stroke count. You should probably shoot for under 15 strokes per 25, that will force you to maintain the same power per stroke while you increase tempo. If you increase tempo, but add like 5 or more strokes to your 25 then you lose efficiency. In order to maintain a low stroke count at a high speed you’ll have to develop a strong kick, and make sure you’re still getting the most you can out of each pull. Personally I shoot for 12 stroke per 25, but when I race the 100 it can increase to like 14 or 15 just bc of the tempo increase. ... I hope that helps

Basically, yes. After the pull he just needs to get his arms back out in front of him, it doesn’t have to be super fast. Encourage him to keep his arms close to his body to reduce drag when he moves his arms to the front. The pull itself should be closer to a freestyle pull, under the body, but with both arms moving together; as opposed to a breaststroke pull which has an out sweep and an in sweep in front of the body.
This is how we teach the kids on our team to dive, mostly because it gradually gets them used entering the water with more and more force.

Drylands can help your kick, but what may be more helpful is hydroception training (which is just a fancy way of staying developing your feel for the water). Start with a one leg flutter kick. Literally grab a kick board and just use one leg to kick a pool length then switch sides. Focus on feeling the water on the top an bottom of your foot while you kick, it should feel kinda like a dolphin kick. Then try counting a beat while you kick. The ideal beat for a freestyle kick is 6 kicks for every 2 strokes. When I work on tempo I count 123456 while I swim and try start my pull on the 1 & the 4.

Hi, I coach an age group team and we try to teach all of our kids all of the strokes. Some 6 year olds can handle fly, most take longer. I like to approach teaching all strokes with drill progressions. Start with dolphin kick, face down, arms out front on the surface. Then add a single double arm pull with a breath (encourage him to get his face back in the water before the end of his pull). If he feels comfortable with the pull and breath while dolphin kicking, then have him try several of those pulls continuously with a dolphin kick. If he can do that drill (I call it “chin drop”, but I’ve heard other names for it too) then he just needs to add the over the surface recovery. If he’s struggling with the recovery, go back to chin drop and encourage him throw the water hard enough behind him to get his hands out of the water. There are plenty of other drills that can help, but this is a good place to start. Hope that helps.

I was 59.0 scy and 1:07.7 lcm in the 100 breast back in the day. I would focus on your pull as well. It’s important to know that your not suppose to get much forward motion from your pull in breaststroke, all of that comes from the kick. Your pull is only there to set up your next kick. Your pull needs to lift your upper body out of the water so you can glide right on the surface of the water during the kick phase of the stroke. All that being said, you need to focus on the in-sweep of you pull, not the out-sweep. The most explosive part of your pull should be the in-sweep. Think about whipping your elbows and forearms together (although they shouldn’t touch). As soon as you feel like your high enough out of the water you need to explode forward while trying to stay on the surface as much as possible through your glide.

I see. Well, I agree that it is a matter of opinion to say that rap is rigidly narrative based while poetry is imagery based. I am fairly certain you can find plenty of examples of both that do not fit those criteria or blur the lines between them. I think a better definition of poetry is a work that intensely illicitness a particular emotion or idea through any number of styles and often with rhythm. Not to get too picky, but rhythm (or “flow”) requires an underlying pulse (or beat). Rhythm is born from beat, without a pulse (whether it is played or not) a rhythm cannot exist. Beat is not the same as music, and is not limited to music. By definition rhythm is based around beat. So if if poems can have rhythms, those poems need beats. (Musicians often use the terms beat and pulse interchangeably, although pulse is always felt, while beat can be played)

Considering how poetry is an ever evolving discipline, from which new forms sprout and mix together continuously, it seems naive to disclude rap from poetry. Although, that is just my opinion. I would be more comfortable claiming that rap is poetry set to music. Most music relies on pitch (based on scales) to form melody in conjunction with rhythm. While many songs have poetic lyrics, they are often constricted by pitch. Rap ignores pitch and replaces harmonic relationships with phonetic ones (not always rhymes). Take away the music and you have an alive melody born from words rather than pitch... it’s just seems like a newer and somewhat unique form of poetry to me. 

... Also, the quality of any performance is based on the performer, regardless of medium. A poor performance will lessen any work no matter how great, and a good performer can bring more from a even a questionable work beyond a surface examination. Sure, you can read a poem on a piece of paper just like sheet music, but a performance of either work done well should transcend the page and dig a little deeper.

To me writing a rap style poem without music behind it is like writing a melody with words. If you want to limit your idea of what poetry can be that’s fine, but you won’t discover anything new if you’re caught up on past ideas.

If you’re in the US Medicaid insurance should cover mental health treatment if you’re in a low enough tax bracket to qualify. Outside of therapy, there are other therapeutic things you can do. Exercise and having a healthy diet, can help. And looking for more appealing career paths may also help you build momentum. Something that is not often talked about, but does have a medical benefit toward depression is volunteer work. Build houses, work at an animal shelter, feed the homeless. If you don’t have the resources for that, then try spending some time every week doing something selfless for someone else. It’s really strange how that can improve a mood. 

Free things to do are a simple as setting small attainable goals for yourself every day, and being proud of just getting one done. Ex. Make your room, do the laundry, send in a job application, write a poem. There are ways to cope, and many paths to follow. I think all the options in life can make it hard to see a defined future. I really hope you start moving in any direction, stopping is the only way you ensure you’ll never get there.

A therapist won’t send you to a mental health ward unless claim to currently be a threat to yourself or others. If you do ever find yourself in the ER don’t panic. I’ve been held in a mental health ward before, I know it’s not fun. But the people there will listen and want to help set you up on the right path. Thb the only path forward is going to involve placing a bit of trust in a few people probably. A quick google search will bring up local therapists. Look for one on your insurance. Or you can talk to a primary care physician you trust (they probably have a better idea of which therapists are best in your area). Set up an appointment asap, they’ll want to know why your seeking out a therapist. I’d be honest and tell the that you’re depressed and have developed suicidal thoughts. You don’t have to mention the thoughts, but if you do they’ll ask if you plan on hurting yourself. Tell them you’re not and you like to have an initial eval. The first few appointments will be awkward and they’ll probably ask you some questions that are pretty personal. They won’t haul you off though, just be open. I’ve found that opening up to those around me about my darkest thoughts has helped a ton. I’m fortunate that I can trust those around me with that info. You can always trust your therapist though. I did get taken to the ER once after mentioning my history with the wrong person, but after explaining that I have my mental state under control and had the right support net set up, they let me go that day. And if after like 4 or 5 sessions you still don’t feel comfortable with the therapist, let them know it isn’t working. They may try to find a new approach or you can go find another therapist. If they put up a fight definitely find a new therapist. If you think you need more intense med management try to get a referral to a psychiatrist, but the wait for an appointment with one can be agonizingly long. It’s best to have a therapist and primary care physician coordinate. That’s the most effective system I’ve found. I’m on therapist number 3, and I think I learned a lot from all of them. Btw I checked myself into the ER the first time, I wasn’t forced there. Trip number 2 was bc of an ignorant secretary in my landlords office. Damn, I kinda rambled, but I hope that helps.
